openingProblem.problem: Both the German Democratic Republic and the People's Republic of China were founded in 1949. By 1991 one had disappeared and the other was trading with its former American enemy. How did the Cold War shape each of them?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: why did the two countries end up so differently?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: The GDR: a state made by the Cold War, 1949–1961
chunks.body:
The German Democratic Republic (GDR) was a product of the Cold War. It was founded in 1949, soon after the West German state, when the Berlin blockade had confirmed the division of Germany. Its fate was decided by the superpowers' rivalry. In May 1952 the Western powers signed treaties binding West Germany to the West and planning its rearmament, rejecting Stalin's offer of a united but unarmed Germany. Moscow and the East German leader **Walter Ulbricht** answered by turning the GDR into a full Soviet satellite.

The economic and social impact was immediate. Under the slogan "Constructing Socialism", farms were forcibly collectivised, private trade and industry were attacked and heavy industry was built up. Collectivisation caused severe food shortages in 1953. The regime also remilitarised, suppressed the churches and persecuted its opponents. Large numbers of East Germans voted with their feet, emigrating through West Berlin.

On 16 June 1953 workers in East Berlin protested against government demands to increase productivity, and within days nearly a million people had joined protests across the country. Soviet forces declared martial law. Judt records that nearly 300 people were killed when Red Army tanks were called in, 1,400 were given long prison sentences and 200 "ringleaders" were shot. The Cold War shaped even the aftermath: the United States handed out $15 million of food in over 5 million "Eisenhower packages", partly to relieve hunger and partly to destabilise Ulbricht's regime.

The exodus continued. By 1958 so many people were leaving through Berlin that Khrushchev issued an ultimatum to the Western powers to leave the city. When that failed, on 13 August 1961, on Ulbricht's orders, a barbed-wire fence went up overnight across Berlin, soon replaced by concrete walls and guard towers. The **Berlin Wall** stopped the flow of migrants and divided families. Judt argues that the Wall reassured East German Communists, who had always feared that Moscow might sell them out.

This mattered because the GDR's economy, society and borders were all shaped by its role as the Soviet bloc's front line, which meant that the state could survive only by locking its own people in.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Cold War decisions in 1952 turned the GDR into a satellite.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Ulbricht pushed for even more collectivisation than Moscow wanted.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Sovietisation caused shortages, repression and the 1953 uprising.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The New Course after Stalin's death tried to relax the pressure.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Mass emigration led to the Berlin Wall.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Wall also reassured the regime that Moscow would not abandon it.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Cold War's social impact on the GDR was to make it a state that had to wall in its own people.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Forced collectivisation, the suppression of churches and food shortages drove East Germans to emigrate through West Berlin, until on 13 August 1961 the Wall stopped them.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the regime survived by force rather than consent, so families were divided and the population was trapped.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the Wall also brought a kind of stability, since the regime no longer feared losing its workforce or being sold out by Moscow.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The Cold War therefore gave the GDR security at the price of freedom.

chunks.title: The GDR behind the Wall, 1961–1990
chunks.body:
Behind the Wall the GDR became one of the most tightly controlled societies in Europe. Its security police, the **Stasi**, grew into a vast apparatus. When its files were opened after 1989, Germans discovered that in addition to 85,000 full-time employees the Stasi had about 60,000 "unofficial collaborators", 110,000 regular informers and more than half a million part-time informers. It held files on 6 million people, one in three of the population. "Husbands spied on wives, professors reported on students, priests informed on their parishioners," Judt writes. "The whole society had in effect been infiltrated."

The GDR's survival rested on Soviet power. In 1989 there were still 360,000 Soviet troops on its soil. Its economy, outsiders believed, was in better shape than its neighbours'. When **Erich Honecker** boasted in October 1989 that the GDR was one of the world's top ten economies, many Western observers believed him; Judt notes that the regime's real efficiency lay in "the manufacture and export of bogus data". The reality emerged after unification: two dwellings in five dated from before 1914, a quarter lacked a bath and more than 60 per cent had no central heating.

Détente brought the GDR international recognition and Western money. Through West Germany's Ostpolitik the two German states signed a Basic Treaty in the early 1970s, and in the 1980s West German subsidies continued while Bonn gave no support to the GDR's internal opposition. Honecker became the first East German leader to visit the Federal Republic, in September 1987. Judt argues that many West German politicians came to share the illusions of the East German leaders they dealt with.

The end came quickly when the Cold War ended. Once Gorbachev made clear that Soviet troops would not defend the regime, East Germans fled again, at one point 2,000 a day. On 9 November 1989 the Wall opened, and on 3 October 1990 the GDR ceased to exist.

This mattered because the GDR had no basis of existence except the Cold War, which meant that when Soviet protection was withdrawn, the state itself disappeared.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: West German subsidies kept the regime afloat.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Ostpolitik had given it international recognition.

chunks.title: China: isolation and the split, 1949–1969
chunks.body:
For the People's Republic of China, the Cold War meant isolation from the West. When the Communists took power in 1949, the United States suspended relations, and for thirty years it recognised the government on Taiwan instead. After China entered the Korean War in late 1950, the US imposed an embargo and worked to isolate Peking. The unfinished civil war with Taiwan became a Cold War flashpoint: in 1954–55 and again in 1958 China's shelling of the offshore islands brought crises with the US, and afterwards the two Chinese sides shelled each other's garrisons on alternate days for twenty years.

The split with the Soviet Union then removed China's main partner. In April 1961 American intelligence reported that the dislocations of Mao's **Great Leap Forward** and "the removal of Soviet technicians" had disrupted China's industrialisation: industrial growth had fallen from about 33 per cent in 1959 to 16 per cent in 1960. The regime faced "the most serious economic difficulties it has confronted" since taking power. Food production in 1960 was little larger than in 1957, although there were about 50 million more people to feed, and China planned to import nearly three million tons of grain in 1961, spending about $200 million of its scarce foreign currency. Public morale, the analysts judged, was at its lowest point since 1949.

China responded with self-reliance and militancy. It built its own atomic bomb, exploded in 1964. Inside China, the split fed the regime's internal struggles: in 1966 American analysts noted that China's internal quarrels were accompanied by mounting violence in polemics against the USSR, part of a campaign against domestic "revisionists" and opponents of Mao. In 1969 another estimate judged that Mao's "ideological pretensions" had earned China the enmity of the USSR and his "bizarre domestic programs" had cost it prestige abroad. After the border clashes of March 1969, the analysts saw "some chance" of a Soviet strike on China's nuclear sites.

This mattered because China faced hostility from both superpowers at once, which meant that the Cold War shaped its economy, its security and the radicalism of its domestic politics.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: China still kept a channel to the US through ambassadorial talks.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Great Leap Forward also caused much of the damage.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Mao's own choices drove domestic radicalism.

chunks.title: Comparing the GDR and China
chunks.body:
After 1969 China's position changed. Fearing the Soviet Union more than the US, it accepted American overtures. In October 1971 it took China's seat at the United Nations from Taiwan; in February 1972 President Nixon visited Beijing; and on 1 January 1979 the two countries established diplomatic relations. Within a month they signed agreements on consular relations, academic exchanges and cooperation in science and technology, and Deng Xiaoping toured the United States. The Cold War, which had isolated China for twenty years, now gave it new partners and access to Western knowledge.

How did the Cold War's impact on the two countries compare?

**Origins.** Both states were born in 1949 out of Cold War divisions: the GDR from the division of Germany, the PRC from a civil war in which the superpowers backed opposite sides. But the GDR was formed from the Soviet zone of occupation, while the Chinese Communists won a civil war.

**Economy.** Both suffered from being cut off from Western trade and from Soviet-style planning: collectivisation caused food shortages in the GDR in 1953, while China's Great Leap Forward and the loss of Soviet technicians produced a deep crisis in 1960–61. But the GDR depended on Soviet troops and, later, West German money, while China, after the split, had to rely on itself.

**Society.** Both regimes used Cold War tension to justify repression. In the GDR the Stasi built a society of informers; in China the split fed campaigns against "revisionists". But East Germans could compare their lives directly with West Germany, which made emigration the GDR's central problem and the Wall its answer.

**Outcome.** The decisive difference was independence. China could change sides in the Cold War, moving from the Soviet camp to cooperation with the US. The GDR could not: it existed only as a Soviet outpost, and when Soviet protection ended in 1989, so did the state.

This mattered because the Cold War affected both countries deeply, which meant that their different degrees of independence from Moscow decided whether they could survive its end.

argumentsThatWork.claim: China used the Cold War triangle to escape isolation.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Relations with the US remained difficult over Taiwan.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Both states suffered economically from Soviet-style planning and isolation.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Domestic choices caused much of the damage.
China was a great power; the GDR never could be.

historiography.argument: The GDR was 'a weak and unloved Communist regime' that Moscow had to shore up; the Stasi's reach meant 'the whole society had in effect been infiltrated'; and the GDR's economic success was largely an illusion built on 'bogus data'.
historiography.useItLikeThis: Judt's view supports the claim that the GDR existed only because of the Cold War, which suggests its collapse in 1989–90 was the logical result of the Cold War's end.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was the GDR's economic weakness a result of Cold War tensions between 1949 and 1989?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: Whether the Cold War, or the planned economy itself, caused the weakness

modelPlan.thesis: Cold War tensions created the GDR's economic system and drained its workforce, but the Soviet-style planned economy itself was the deeper cause, and Western subsidies and bogus data concealed the weakness until 1989.

arguments.claim: Cold War origins: the 1952 decision to Sovietise (named factor first).
Illusion: bogus data and West German subsidies.

modelPlan.counter: Collectivisation and central planning were choices of the regime, which Moscow at times tried to moderate.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Would the GDR's economy have been weak without the Cold War? The question is hard to answer, because without the Cold War the GDR would not have existed.

segments.text: Cold War tensions created the GDR's economic weakness by imposing a Soviet system and draining its workforce.
After the Western treaties of 1952 the GDR was forcibly collectivised, causing food shortages, and until 1961 its people emigrated through West Berlin.
This meant that the GDR lost skilled workers and suffered the inefficiencies of central planning, so its economy lagged behind West Germany's.
However, the planned economy was itself a cause, and West German subsidies and 'bogus data' hid the weakness until 1989.
Cold War tensions were therefore the root of the GDR's weakness, because they produced both the system and the state.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “China gained more than it lost from the Cold War.” Discuss with reference to the period 1949 to 1979.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The claim: China gained more than it lost
decodeKey.judgement: Gains against losses, and by what criterion

modelPlan.thesis: China lost heavily in the 1950s and 1960s through war, isolation and the loss of Soviet help, but by 1979 it had used the Cold War triangle to gain a UN seat, US recognition and access to Western science, so the claim holds only for the end of the period.

arguments.claim: Against: isolation and the US embargo.
For: the UN seat and Nixon's visit.

modelPlan.counter: China's own policies, such as the Great Leap Forward, caused much of its loss, not the Cold War.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: By what criterion? Position in 1979 shows gain; cost over thirty years shows loss.

segments.text: China lost more than it gained from the Cold War for most of the period, but gained by its end.
The US embargo from 1950 and the removal of Soviet technicians around 1960 cut China off from both camps, and industrial growth fell from 33 to 16 per cent.
This meant that China paid a heavy price for its position between the superpowers, so it faced its worst crisis since 1949.
However, by 1979 China had the UN seat, relations with the US and agreements on science and academic exchange.
The claim is therefore valid only for the end of the period, when China turned Cold War rivalry to its advantage.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the impact of Cold War tensions on the GDR and China between 1949 and 1979.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.scope: The impact of Cold War tensions

modelPlan.thesis: Both states were shaped economically and socially by the Cold War, but China's independence let it change sides and escape isolation, whereas the GDR remained a Soviet outpost that walled in its own people.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both born of Cold War divisions in 1949.
Similarity: economic damage from Soviet-style planning.
Difference: emigration and the Wall in the GDR.

modelPlan.counter: Both regimes used Cold War tension to justify repression, so their societies were affected in similar ways.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? Independence: China could change camps, the GDR could not.

segments.text: The Cold War shaped both the GDR and China, but in very different ways.
Both suffered from Soviet-style planning, with food shortages in the GDR in 1953 and a deep crisis in China in 1960–61, whereas only the GDR had to build a Wall in 1961 to stop its people leaving.
This meant that the GDR's central problem was its direct comparison with West Germany, while China's was isolation from both superpowers.
However, China escaped isolation by changing sides, establishing relations with the US in 1979, which the GDR could never do.
The decisive difference was therefore independence from Moscow, which decided each state's fate.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the social impact of the Cold War on the GDR between 1949 and 1989.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge

modelPlan.thesis: The Cold War's social impact on the GDR was severe: repression, mass emigration, divided families and a society penetrated by the Stasi; the Wall brought stability only by trapping the population.

arguments.claim: The Stasi and a society of informers.

modelPlan.counter: The Wall gave the regime stability after 1961, and détente brought recognition and contacts with the West.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which impact was most significant? Surveillance, because it reached into every family.

segments.text: The Cold War's most significant social impact on the GDR was the penetration of society by the Stasi.
The Stasi had 85,000 staff and over half a million part-time informers, and held files on one in three East Germans.
This meant that the regime, unable to win consent after 1953 and walled in after 1961, controlled its people through fear and suspicion.
However, the Wall also brought a stability that allowed the regime to win international recognition through Ostpolitik.
The Cold War therefore produced a society that was stable on the surface but, in Judt's words, 'infiltrated, atomized and polluted'.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the causes and consequences of the Sino-Soviet split for China between 1958 and 1969.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The split grew from rivalry for leadership and Soviet refusal of nuclear help; for China its consequences were economic damage, self-reliance including a bomb, domestic radicalism and, by 1969, fear of Soviet attack.

arguments.claim: Cause: Soviet refusal of nuclear help (see P2-12-SINO).
Consequence: loss of Soviet technicians and economic crisis.
Consequence: radicalism and fear of attack.

modelPlan.counter: The Great Leap Forward caused much of the economic damage independently of the split.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? China's search for a new partner, which led to the US.

segments.text: For China, the split's most important consequence was the loss of its only great-power partner.
In 1961 US analysts reported that the removal of Soviet technicians, with the Great Leap Forward, had cut industrial growth from 33 to 16 per cent.
This meant that China had to rely on itself, building its own atomic bomb in 1964, while the split fed campaigns against 'revisionists' at home.
However, the Great Leap Forward was Mao's own policy, so the split was not the only cause of China's crisis.
The split therefore pushed China towards self-reliance, radicalism and, by 1969, fear of a Soviet attack that would lead it to the US.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the economic impact of the Cold War on China between 1949 and 1979.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: How each phase of the Cold War affected China's economy

modelPlan.thesis: The Cold War cut China off first from Western trade and then from Soviet help, deepening an economic crisis that the Great Leap Forward had begun; only after 1979 did it bring access to Western science and exchanges.
modelPlan.counter: Domestic policy, especially the Great Leap Forward, shaped China's economy as much as the Cold War did.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: How did the phases connect? Isolation from the West made Soviet help vital, so its loss in 1960 was all the more damaging.

segments.text: The Cold War damaged China's economy by cutting it off first from the West and then from the USSR.
The US embargo dated from the Korean War, and in 1960 Soviet technicians were removed, so industrial growth fell from 33 to 16 per cent.
This meant that China, having relied on Soviet expertise because the West was closed to it, faced its worst crisis since 1949.
However, the Great Leap Forward and bad weather also caused the crisis, as US analysts noted in 1961.
The Cold War therefore deepened China's economic problems until 1979, when changing sides brought new access to Western science.
